documents: Nakamura et al. (2022), Structural anomaly at the boundary between strong and weak plate coupling in the central-western Nankai Trough, Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL098180 (published PDF, 9 pp.; supporting information not supplied)

entry.evidence: therefore, it is important to understand the structural factors defining this boundary.

sequences.source_document: Nakamura et al. 2022, GRL, published PDF

steps.action: Posed the question of which structural factors are associated with variations in megathrust slip behaviour, and with the seismogenic–transition boundary, in the central-western Nankai Trough, where slip, slow-earthquake and coupling distributions are known.
steps.quote: To investigate the structural factors associated with slip behavior on the megathrust fault, we conducted seismic reflection surveys

steps.action: Listed published candidate controls on slip behaviour: fault-rock properties, pore-pressure anomalies, and subducting-plate roughness.
steps.quote: Several key elements have been proposed to control the spatiotemporal variation of slip behavior on the plate boundary

steps.action: Acquired densely spaced seismic reflection lines (4–8 km spacing) on three cruises (2018–2020) with large sources and 4–5.5 km streamers, reprocessed 1997/1999 data, and depth-converted short-streamer profiles to fill gaps.
steps.quote: The primary datasets were obtained by three dedicated seismic surveys

steps.action: Processed the data by Kirchhoff PreSDM with velocity models built from RMS velocities, tomography and forward modeling. Deep velocities were set to a uniform value chosen from 3–6 km/s by visual inspection (4 km/s), with 5 km/s below the plate top.
steps.quote: The reflection data were processed by Kirchhoff prestack depth migration (PreSDM)

steps.action: Read the depth profiles: the top of the subducting plate (basement) and the fold-and-thrust structure with a decollement are traced in most profiles.
steps.quote: Reflections of the top of the subducting Philippine Sea plate (referred to hereafter as the basement) can be traced in most of the profiles

steps.action: Gridded the picked basement depths with a nearest-neighbour algorithm into a basement depth map (Figure 3a).
steps.quote: The basement depths in the profiles were gridded with the nearest neighbor algorithm

steps.action: Compared the depth map with earlier plate models and a regional tomography. The map is generally consistent, but 0.5–1.5 km shallower landward, which the authors attribute to their lower overriding-plate velocities.
steps.quote: The result is generally consistent with earlier models of the subducting plate

steps.action: Checked previously reported subducted seamounts off Cape Muroto (Kodaira 2000, Park 1999) against the new basement map: both appear as features A and B.
steps.quote: We also confirmed the presence of another subducted seamount reported by a previous reflection study

steps.action: Identified new possible subducted seamounts (C, D) and NNW-SSE grabens in the incoming plate (E, F), interpreting the grabens with cited work.
steps.quote: Local basement highs off Kii Channel may also be subducting seamounts that have not been previously reported

steps.action: Produced a residual basement depth map by subtracting a 0.5° boxcar-smoothed depth map from the gridded map.
steps.quote: we produced a residual depth map (Figure 3b) by subtracting a smoothed basement depth (Figure S7)

steps.action: Found in the residual map a narrow arcuate depression extending intermittently for about 100 km along the bathymetric Tosabae Trough, from off Kii Channel to off central Tosa Bay.
steps.quote: a narrow, arcuate depression that appears to extend intermittently over ∼100 km

steps.action: Posed two rivals: a true basement depression, or a velocity anomaly in the overriding plate that the reflection-based velocity model cannot resolve.
steps.quote: this arcuate feature may represent velocity anomalies within the overlying plate along the Tosabae Trough rather than a basement depression

steps.action: Compared the rivals with published refraction and tomography models. Line SK01 shows a hanging-wall low-velocity zone beneath the Tosabae Trough, but only along one line, and a 3D tomography low-velocity area does not coincide with the anomaly.
steps.quote: shows a low-velocity zone down to ∼5 km depth within the hanging wall beneath the Tosabae Trough

steps.action: Kept the existence of an anomaly along the Tosabae Trough while leaving both interpretations open, because the velocity models have little horizontal variation above the feature.
steps.quote: Regardless of their interpretation, our seismic data analysis and basement mapping strongly suggest the presence of an anomaly along the Tosabae Trough.

steps.action: Compared the depression rival with fault-offset basement imaged by Tsuji et al. (2013) to the east: no such faults or strong reflections are imaged beneath the putative depression here.
steps.quote: no such faults or strong reflections were imaged within the subducting plate beneath the putative depression

steps.action: Considered a basement low around a subducting seamount chain whose backthrusts would deform the hanging wall and lower its velocity. Preferred the hanging-wall low-velocity-zone interpretation.
steps.quote: we prefer the interpretation that a low-velocity zone exists in the hanging wall along the Tosabae Trough

steps.action: Compared the anomaly's location with the 1946 rupture area, the slow-earthquake zone, the Obara & Kato (2016) zone model, and the geodetic coupling map: it lies at the strong–weak coupling boundary.
steps.quote: The structural anomaly also closely corresponds to the boundary between regions of strong and weak interplate coupling

steps.action: Speculated on an origin: a KBEFZ-like fault zone, possibly strike-slip, whose fracturing lowers velocity, bounding a high-density landward hanging wall (gravity anomaly) that may favour strong coupling.
steps.quote: we speculate that a fault zone similar to the KBEFZ may underlie the Tosabae Trough

steps.action: Compared slow-earthquake locations with individual subducted seamounts and found no clear link. Suggested instead that the oblique subduction of a large basement bulge damaged the seaward hanging wall.
steps.quote: are not clearly connected to the individual seamounts in our map of basement topography

steps.action: Summarized the claim: the arcuate anomaly, preferably a hanging-wall low-velocity zone possibly due to faulting, lies at the strong–weak coupling boundary. Called for further investigation.
steps.quote: This anomaly is located at the boundary between areas of the strong and weak interplate coupling.

tree.answer: Structural factors at the seismogenic–transition boundary; an arcuate anomaly along the Tosabae Trough emerges from the maps
No; the basement is imaged through PreSDM with a poorly constrained deep velocity model
Map plate-boundary structure and correlate it with known slip and coupling zones
Basement depression versus low-velocity zone in the hanging wall
Only partly; reflection data cannot separate them, and sparse refraction and tomography data partly can
Found: natural subduction-zone structure imaged by surveys
Partly; the map agrees with earlier plate models, but LVZ support comes from one refraction line and a tomography model mismatches
Anomaly kept; LVZ interpretation preferred, depression not excluded
Not assessable; no review file supplied

end.claim: An arcuate structural anomaly about 100 km long along the Tosabae Trough lies at the boundary between strong and weak interplate coupling, and is preferably interpreted as a low-velocity zone in the overriding plate, possibly from faulting at the updip edge of the seismogenic zone.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the residual basement depth map built from the densely spaced PreSDM profiles, the arcuate anomaly along the Tosabae Trough would not have been seen.

gates.evidence: Action: a broad question, not a stated hypothesis, directed the dense survey design (p. 2), and the anomaly and its rivals arose after mapping (pp. 5-6). Claim: the anomaly–coupling coincidence and the LVZ preference were set against independent refraction and tomography data that could have disagreed (and partly did: Yamamoto et al. 2017, p. 7), but the depression rival was not excluded. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed in advance; the deep velocity (4 km/s) was chosen by visual inspection of the processed images (p. 3).

imports.item: Parabolic Radon transform filtering for multiple and noise suppression
Boxcar (moving-average) filter to separate regional and residual basement depth
Kirchhoff PreSDM processing performed by DownUnder GeoSolutions

novelty_claims.quote: Our depth map allows the basement to be visualized in unprecedented detail.
Local basement highs off Kii Channel may also be subducting seamounts that have not been previously reported
C and D indicate possible subducted seamounts found in this study.
Our densely spaced seismic reflection data set reveals the detailed basement topography without relying on interpolation between sparse datasets.

disagreements.target: Earlier subducting-plate models (Baba et al., 2002; Nakanishi et al., 2018)
disagreements.support: The dense reflection depth map places the landward plate 0.5-1.5 km shallower, attributed to lower overriding-plate velocities in the PreSDM model.
disagreements.quote: the absolute depth of the subducting plate is 0.5–1.5 km shallower than in the previous models

disagreements.target: Velocity estimates of previous refraction seismic studies (Nakanishi et al., 2018; Qin et al., 2021)
disagreements.support: The PreSDM velocities in the deeper overriding plate are lower than the refraction values, though the paper also says deep velocities are poorly constrained by its streamer length.
disagreements.quote: our velocity estimate of ∼3.3–3.9 km/s (Figures S1–S4) is ∼10%–25% lower than estimates by previous refraction seismic studies

disagreements.target: Studies linking slow earthquakes to subducting seamounts and roughness (e.g., Wang & Bilek, 2011; Sun et al., 2020)
disagreements.support: VLFE and slow slip locations are scattered along the trough axis and do not match individual seamounts on the new basement map.
disagreements.quote: are not clearly connected to the individual seamounts in our map of basement topography

alternatives_considered.chosen: Uniform velocity of 4 km/s for regions with velocities above 3 km/s
alternatives_considered.reason: Visual inspection of the reflection from the top of the subducting oceanic plate

alternatives_considered.chosen: Low-velocity zone in the hanging wall along the Tosabae Trough
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Basement depression in the subducting plate surface (possibly a low around a subducting seamount chain)
alternatives_considered.reason: Refraction line SK01 shows a hanging-wall low-velocity zone; no basement faults imaged beneath the depression; comparison with the eastern Nankai Trough (KBEFZ)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Faulting/fracturing in the hanging wall (KBEFZ-like fault zone) causing low velocity
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Strike-slip fault zone like the Median Tectonic Line; deformation from backthrusts at the leading flank of a subducting seamount chain
